# Closing report: E-commerce Funnel Analytics

**Status: closed.** The project closes at release v1.1.3, which adds this report and the `/questions` page to the v1.1.2 analysis; no analysis changed after v1.1.2. Generated by `python -m funnel.closing` from the owner-approved content in `ai-workflow/closing-content.md` and the committed exports. Every figure below is read from its export field; none is typed. Don't edit this file by hand.

The business question was: **where in the view-to-purchase funnel do sessions most often end with no observed purchase, which categories hold the most carted value with no observed purchase in the session, and what should the team test first?** The project answered the first part descriptively, investigated two open questions in the numbers, and stopped short of ranking categories when the pre-registered method failed its own check. Its answer to "what should the team test first?" is question 1 below.

## 2. What is established

- **The funnel as observed.** Session counts, view, cart, and purchase steps, purchase paths, and category funnels for October 2019 (UTC), computed only as defined in `docs/metrics.md`. Every published number was independently reproduced (R2) before it was published.
- **Where the two revenue figures differ.** The difference sits entirely in repeated purchase events of the same product within a session, and its breakdown is published (analysis A).
- **What happened to carted value with no observed purchase in the session, within a week.** Part of it was followed by a purchase of the same product by the same user in a later session, for sessions early enough to have a full week of follow-up (analysis B). This qualifies how the carted-value figure can be read; it doesn't measure value that could be gained.
- **A method result.** The pre-registered category ranking would have reported differences between categories that were identical by construction, so it was not published (F4).

## 3. What is not established

- **Any cause.** Every finding describes October 2019. None shows what a change to the funnel would cause; only an experiment can (question 8).
- **What repeated purchase events are.** Extra units, or the same purchase logged again: the data can't tell, so every revenue figure is shown both ways (question 2; uncertainty U1).
- **Whether one `user_id` is one person.** Findings that link sessions assume it. The checks the data allows passed, but cross-device identity can't be verified from this file (question 3; U2).
- **Anything after the observed window.** Purchases after the week measured, or after October 2019, aren't observed (questions 4 and 5).
- **Which categories differ in conversion.** The ranking was stopped; no category is described as better or worse than another (question 6).
- **Profit.** The data has no margins or returns (question 9).

## 4. The F6 lesson: test the rule before trusting it

Sprint 3 pre-registered a size-adjusted category ranking with a negative control: shuffle the category labels, and the rule should find no differences. The control failed. To tell a code bug from a flawed method, the rule was run on synthetic data where every category had the same rate by construction, using the committed code at the real settings. It still reported differences, with no clustering and no shuffling involved. The flaw is in the rule itself: bootstrap intervals for ranks reproduce a chance ordering when categories are tied, so chance extremes look separable. Nothing from the ranking was published (`docs/metrics.md`, Changes entry of 2026-09-27; escalation brief, §2).

The lesson for any later work: **calibrate a decision rule on synthetic data with a known answer before it touches real data.** A negative control is worth pre-registering because it can fail; this one did its job.

## 5. The unknown-actor incident

On 2026-09-27, while a ranking run was in progress, an unidentified actor made changes that neither the project owner nor Claude Code made. There is no trace of them in any Claude Code transcript or in Claude desktop data. The changes:

- edited the staging models to exclude one user;
- added a Changes entry to the metric contract that falsely claimed the owner's approval;
- rebuilt the warehouse outside the gated build;
- ran the ranking on the result.

Claude Code caught the mismatch at run reconciliation, when the run's recorded memory gate and marts fingerprint didn't match the run the owner had started.

**What was done:**

- **Quarantine:** everything was preserved, unmerged, on the branch `quarantine/unapproved-2026-09-27`.
- **Restore:** the committed state was restored and rebuilt through the gated build. Its fingerprint matched the marts from before the incident.
- **Guards:** new run guards refuse a dirty working tree, and refuse marts without a gated build record (`funnel.provenance`).
- **Records:** the correction log records the incident with the origin "Unattributed second actor". The escalation brief has the full timeline.
